q: What does the one-task assertion verify in the supplied experiment?
options: The given six fixed inputs produce one local effect
The full production approval service authenticates every responder
Any repeated event remains idempotent across a service restart
Network isolation was applied to a real endpoint once
explanation: The simulator checks one in-memory run over fictional data.

q: Why predict expected results before running the program?
options: To create a case even when the fixture has no stable ID
To make every outcome match the last observed run without review
To avoid inspecting the script's output during review
To compare actual behaviour against a stated contract
explanation: Predictions make it easier to spot surprising or incorrect results.

q: The out-of-scope target's fixture says approved. Why does it still produce no task?
options: The training system assumes every unfamiliar target already has a task
Approval validity is determined by whether a result uses a dash
The permitted target check blocks it before evaluating approval
All input labels are treated as synonyms for the original target
explanation: Approval for a record cannot make an unapproved scope eligible.

q: What data identifies a stable mock effect in this script?
options: The current line number in the displayed audit trail
The event, target and training operation tuple
The random user name of whoever opened the worksheet
The total number of cases received before the current one
explanation: The tuple distinguishes the specific intended training task.

q: A return code says the script succeeded but the last four rows unexpectedly show IDs. What next?
options: Treat the branch results as wrong despite the process status
Accept the run because the program ended without a runtime error
Count the displayed IDs as independent approvals
Change the worksheet expected values to match the live output
explanation: The test should verify both effect identity and individual branch output.

q: Which row creates T-001 in the original run?
options: The denied A-19 receipt for LAB-42 in the same fixture
The A-18 receipt waiting for an approver's response
The repeated A-17 after T-001 already exists
The first approved A-17 receipt for LAB-41
explanation: The first eligible record creates the only new training task.

q: A later input is valid and has a different event ID for the same target. What follows under the current effect key?
options: It must link to A-17 because its target shares a name
It is automatically out of scope because LAB-41 was seen
It can create a distinct training task
It always lacks approval because another event used that target
explanation: A different event ID changes the tuple even when the target is shared.

q: Which fixture row remains waiting for a decision?
options: A-20 whose target is outside the approved set
A-18 for the allowed LAB-43 target
The event-less receipt for LAB-41 that lacks its identity
A-19 whose decision is already a denial
explanation: A-18 is eligible input with a pending approval state.

q: Running the unchanged script again reports one new task. What does that say about persistence?
options: Its local state resets between process runs
The original training task was persisted and discovered across restarts
The case service successfully deleted the prior training task
The new run performed a protective action on the same live asset
explanation: The in-memory dictionary is initialised empty in each execution.

q: What does a dash in the task ID field indicate?
options: A verified deletion of an existing task from a case service
A change that must complete without any additional evidence
A synthetic account approval that applies to all future operations
No task reference for that audited input
explanation: Stopped or pending branches have no training task.

q: The worksheet counts two effects because A-17 has two rows. How should it be corrected?
options: Remove the repeat receipt so every audit row creates a task
Count every approved fixture even if no effect could occur
Count the distinct task ID and retain both receipt rows
Create a new real case task to make the original count match
explanation: Multiple receipts can refer to one effect without making another.

q: What should a lab completion statement identify?
options: The names and credentials of all real workflow operators
The fixed inputs, observed result and simulator limits
The production service's exact authority in the real team
A claim that every future integration will behave identically
explanation: A narrow statement ties evidence to the conditions actually tested.

q: A misspelled status enters the current script. What happens finding-wise?
options: No task; the generic not-approved state needs interpretation
It becomes approved because it is neither denied nor pending
It becomes an existing task whenever the asset label was used earlier
It retries until the fixture provides an approved version
explanation: Unknown values cannot cause an effect, but logging their reason can improve.

q: What is the intended role of the two review-input rows?
options: Demonstrate two approvals for the same accepted target
Prove that all tasks were sent through a public connector
Supply two alternate sites for an unauthorised fallback lookup
Show two invalid inputs stop without effects
explanation: Invalid scope and missing identity need review instead of a change.

q: A paper variation loses acknowledgment after a possible remote effect. Which status fits?
options: No effect confirmed solely from the missing receipt
Verified effect inferred from the approving role's decision
Effect unknown, with a reconciliation owner
Newly authorised repeat request before inspecting the target
explanation: The missing acknowledgment leaves the result unresolved until a permitted check can confirm the actual effect.

q: Which dependency would production restart-safe handling require?
options: A local dictionary recreated for every new process
Persistent effect history or authoritative reconciliation
A new random key that differs for duplicate events
A count of approved requests shown only on one worker
explanation: A durable record is needed to distinguish existing effects after a restart.

q: The revised version reports one task but the pending fixture was logged as denied. What changed?
options: The overall effect count passed but branch reporting regressed
The whole test passed because pending and denial are equivalent
The expected count should increase to include unresolved decisions
The denial is validated by the case effect's existence elsewhere
explanation: Audit states must distinguish different decisions even when neither creates an effect.

q: What should a peer check for A-20 specifically?
options: It used the same approved target as both prior A-17 receipts
Its effect ID was printed in the first line of the script
The denial code proves that every target was independently reviewed
The target was rejected and no task exists
explanation: The out-of-scope target must remain blocked independently of its status.

q: The class wants to compare versions with renamed statuses. What preserves comparability?
options: Treat different labels as automatically equivalent if they appear on the same row
Change the number of samples until both final counts are equal
Map states deliberately and keep original fixture expectations
Remove the audit states and compare only the time the scripts finished
explanation: The mapping must preserve different conditions and effects for comparison.

q: What information accompanies pending approval in a real handoff?
options: The unverified claim that protection already took effect
The responsible role, decision location and review timing
The original notification with no access to current decision status
The case owner's personal confirmation code for use by later shifts
explanation: A pending record needs an actionable decision route.

q: The lab result is summarised as six defensive actions executed. What should replace it?
options: Six inputs audited and one training task created
All invalid and denied actions were executed but not logged
Three effects because three records included the approved value
Six verified protective effects because each row printed a status
explanation: Audit rows count inputs and do not each indicate a state change.

q: Which check goes beyond the task count alone?
options: Check that every line uses the same console indentation
Verify the last run printed exactly one copy of the source code
Guess the meaning of the outcome from the data order alone
Confirm the expected status and ID for each input
explanation: Per-input expectations reveal branch and mapping regressions that can leave the total effect count unchanged.

q: A peer asks whether an approved status from an incident can be trusted directly in production. What is the answer?
options: Accept any text that matches the simulator's approved value
Allow the source to grant authority for new targets itself
Verify against a trusted decision, authority and scope
Assume the case has an authorised approval whenever an ID exists
explanation: The fixture models authority and does not implement authorisation.

q: What should a reviewer retain to reproduce this experiment?
options: Only a screenshot showing one favourable task count
The exact script version, fixture and observed output
The production connector passwords used in another training run
The name of a different service supporting the same workflow concept
explanation: A reviewer needs the tested input and execution evidence.

q: Which exercise variation tests prevention of unstated approval states?
options: Replace a pending status with an unknown value and check zero tasks
Change the display order of the output table only
Repeat a context explanation without changing any input
Choose a live device to test whether reaction timing improves
explanation: The proposed variation checks a concrete rejected-state behaviour.
